Eggs of the Buff-throated woodcreeper are estimated to have an initial wet weight of approximately 6.84 grams [Ww0 = approximately 6.84 grams], a value derived from the geometric mean of typical egg dimensions measuring 27 millimeters in length and 22 millimeters in width. This modest starting mass reflects the relatively small yolk volume characteristic of altricial passerines, which rely predominantly on parental provisioning after hatching. The incubating adult maintains the embryonated egg at a mean temperature of 32 °C [T = 32 °C], a thermal regime that supports a developmental period culminating in hatching after approximately 16 days [ab = approximately 16 days]. This incubation duration, while broadly consistent with that reported for the congeneric species Xiphorhynchus elegans, positions the woodcreeper within the expected range for a bird of its body plan, balancing the energetic costs of extended thermoregulation against the benefits of producing a well-developed hatchling capable of rapid post-natal growth.

Following successful hatching, the altricial nestling experiences a period of intense parental care within the cavity nest. The developmental trajectory under typical thermal conditions at 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C] culminates in fledging, defined as the achievement of first flight, at approximately 18.5 days after hatching [tx = approximately 18.5 days after hatching], a timeline comparable to that noted for the Elegant woodcreeper. This relatively brief nestling phase is characteristic of many tropical insectivores, where predation pressure on cavity nests may select for rapid feather maturation and early departure. The downy chick undergoes a swift transition from a pin-feathered nestling to a fledgling precursor, with the calcification of flight feathers proceeding rapidly. During this period, the developing chick relies entirely on the provisioning behavior of both parents, which deliver arthropod prey at high rates to meet the substantial metabolic demands of tissue accretion and thermoregulatory development.

Reproductive investment in the Buff-throated woodcreeper is characterized by a modest annual output. Females typically lay one to three eggs per clutch [N_R_i = one to three eggs per clutch], and available field records indicate that they produce a single clutch each year [F_R_i = a single clutch each year], a reproductive strategy consistent with the low fecundity observed in many Neotropical suboscines. This annual reproductive schedule, when maintained at a body temperature of 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C], represents a maximum reproductive rate that is considerably lower than that of temperate-zone passerines, likely reflecting the constraints imposed by a stable but resource-limited tropical environment. The trade-off between current and future reproduction is evident in this conservative strategy, which allocates substantial parental effort to a limited number of offspring per breeding season, maximizing per-capita survival rather than maximizing the total number of independent offspring produced.

Sexual maturation in this species occurs following an extended juvenile period. Based on comparative data for the genus, and under the physiological conditions typical of active individuals maintained at 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C], the age since birth at puberty is approximately 55.5 days [tp = approximately 55.5 days]. However, the age at first reproduction is substantially later, with individuals typically initiating their first successful breeding attempt at approximately 547.5 days since birth [tR = approximately 547.5 days since birth] at a temperature of 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C]. This pronounced delay between the attainment of gonadal maturity and the commencement of actual breeding activity is a common feature among birds that require extended time to acquire a high-quality territory or to develop the foraging skills necessary to sustain the energetic demands of egg production and chick provisioning. The subadult bird therefore spends a considerable portion of its early life in a pre-reproductive juvenile phase, refining its bark-gleaning techniques on the trunks of mature forest trees.

Respirometry trials at a core body temperature of 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C] revealed a maximal resting metabolic rate of 94.55 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 94.55 milliliters of oxygen per hour], while a concurrent measurement under slightly lower activity conditions registered 80.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 80.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. These metabolic rates are broadly consistent with those predicted for a bird of its body mass, which in adult females reaches an ultimate wet weight of approximately 59.7 grams [Wwi = approximately 59.7 grams], a figure situated within the published range of 49 to 74 grams. The maximum longevity recorded for this species, again under the thermal regime of 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C], is approximately 10 years [am = approximately 10 years], a lifespan that ranks among the longest documented for dendrocolaptids of comparable body size and underscores the slow pace of life in this tropical lineage.
